title: PAUL SAID FAITH ALONE. JAMES SAID FAITH WITHOUT WORKS IS DEAD. SO WHO WAS RIGHT?
paragraphs: PAUL SAID FAITH ALONE. JAMES SAID FAITH WITHOUT WORKS IS DEAD. SO WHO WAS RIGHT?
Two Apostles. Two Statements That Seem to Contradict Each Other. One Gospel That Could Change Everything You Thought You Knew About Salvation.

What if two of the most misunderstood verses in the Bible have caused some Christians to live in fear of losing their salvation… while allowing others to live comfortably in sins they have never truly surrendered?
One person lies awake at night wondering whether they have done enough good things for God to accept them.
Another sleeps peacefully, convinced that because they once prayed a prayer, it no longer matters how they live.
Both open their Bibles.
One reads Paul.
“Therefore we conclude that a man is justified by faith without the deeds of the law.” — Romans 3:28 (KJV)
The other reads James.
“Ye see then how that by works a man is justified, and not by faith only.” — James 2:24 (KJV)
Wait.
Read those verses again.
Paul says a person is justified by faith apart from works of the law.
James says a person is justified by works and not by faith alone.
These are not obscure statements buried in forgotten corners of Scripture. They are direct declarations from two men whose writings belong to the inspired Word of God.
And if you have ever wondered how both can be true, you are not alone.
Because beneath this apparent contradiction lies something far more personal than a theological debate.
It is a question that reaches into your private life, your hidden struggles, your unspoken guilt, and the parts of your heart nobody sees.
Are you trusting your good behavior to save you… or are you using God's grace as an excuse to remain unchanged?
That question matters.
Because you can spend your entire life trying to earn a salvation Jesus already purchased.
And you can spend your entire life claiming to possess a faith that has never truly taken hold of your heart.
Neither is the freedom Christ came to give.
But to understand why Paul and James are not enemies, we must first understand something many people miss.
They are confronting two different spiritual dangers.
And they are asking two different questions.
Paul is confronting the person who believes obedience can earn acceptance before God.
James is confronting the person who claims to believe in God while remaining indifferent to the obedience that genuine faith produces.
Paul is asking, “How is a sinner declared righteous before God?”
James is asking, “What kind of faith is genuine, and how does it reveal itself?”
And suddenly, what looked like a contradiction begins to expose two different ways the human heart can misunderstand grace.
Imagine a man standing before God, carrying every sin he has ever committed.
The lies.
The lust.
The bitterness.
The pride.
The cruel words he wishes he could take back.
The promises he made to God and broke before the week was over.
He has no defense.
So he begins explaining his good deeds.
He attended church.
He gave money to the poor.
He helped his neighbors.
He volunteered.
He tried to become a better person.
But the question is not whether he has ever done anything good.
The question is whether any of those deeds can erase his guilt before a perfectly holy God.
They cannot.
This is the spiritual danger Paul confronts.
In Romans 3:23, he writes:
All.
Not merely the scandalous sinner whose failures became public.
Not merely the person struggling with addiction, sexual immorality, dishonesty, or rebellion.
All.
The respected church leader.
The generous businessman.
The devoted parent.
The person who has memorized entire chapters of Scripture.
Every human being stands in need of grace.
And Paul refuses to let anyone imagine that religious performance can purchase what only Christ can provide.
In Ephesians 2:8–9, he writes:
Look carefully at that word grace.
In the original Greek, Paul uses χάρις (charis).
Grace.
Favor given freely, not wages earned by deserving workers.
And when Paul speaks of faith, he uses πίστις (pistis), a word that, depending on context, carries the sense of faith, trust, or faithfulness.
In Ephesians 2:8, the emphasis is not on human achievement but on salvation received through faith.
The sinner does not arrive at the cross holding a résumé of righteousness.
The sinner comes empty-handed.
And Christ is sufficient.
That is why Romans 5:1 declares:
“Therefore being justified by faith, we have peace with God through our Lord Jesus Christ.” (KJV)
The Greek word translated justified is δικαιωθέντες (dikaiōthentes), from the verb δικαιόω (dikaioō).
In this context, it speaks of being declared righteous before God.
Not because the sinner has suddenly lived a flawless life.
Not because the sinner has finally accumulated enough good deeds.
But because of Jesus Christ.
His sinless life.
His sacrificial death.
His resurrection.
His finished work.
This is why the cross is not merely an inspiring example of love.
It is the place where Christ bore the judgment sinners deserved.
As Paul writes in 2 Corinthians 5:21:
Jesus did not die to help us become good enough to save ourselves.
He died because we could never save ourselves.
And that is where the scandal becomes grace.
The guilty are offered forgiveness.
The condemned are invited into reconciliation.
The spiritually bankrupt receive riches they could never earn.
But now comes the part that makes some people uncomfortable.
Because James opens his letter and begins confronting a different kind of person.
Not someone desperately trying to earn salvation.
Someone claiming to possess saving faith while showing no concern for what God commands.
Someone who knows the correct religious language.
Someone who can say, “I believe in Jesus.”
Someone who can quote Scripture.
Someone who can sound spiritually mature in public.
But when another person is hungry, hurting, or desperate for help, their faith never moves beyond words.
James asks:
“What doth it profit, my brethren, though a man say he hath faith, and have not works? can faith save him?” — James 2:14 (KJV)
Notice the wording.
James is examining a person who says he has faith.
That distinction is crucial.
He is not teaching that salvation must be purchased through good behavior.
He is questioning whether a verbal claim of faith, unsupported by any evidence of a transformed life, is genuine saving faith at all.
Then he gives an example that is almost painfully ordinary.
A brother or sister lacks proper clothing and daily food.
Someone sees the need and offers kind religious words.
Be warm.
Be filled.
Go in peace.
But they do nothing to help.
James asks what good those words accomplish.
And then he delivers the statement that has unsettled generations of readers.
“Even so faith, if it hath not works, is dead, being alone.” — James 2:17 (KJV)
Dead.
Not merely weak.
Not merely immature.
Dead.
In Greek, the word is νεκρά (nekra).
Lifeless.
James is not saying that good works manufacture saving faith.
He is saying that a claimed faith with no living expression is like a body without breath.
It has the appearance of something that should be alive.
But something essential is missing.
And this is where the conversation becomes personal.
Because there is a difference between struggling against sin and making peace with sin.
There is a difference between falling and refusing to repent.
There is a difference between a wounded believer crying out for mercy and someone deliberately using mercy as permission to continue in rebellion.
A genuine Christian can struggle terribly.
Peter denied Jesus three times.
David committed grievous sin.
The Corinthian church had serious problems requiring correction.
Scripture never teaches that genuine believers instantly become incapable of failure.
But neither does Scripture present saving faith as a mere statement that leaves the heart permanently indifferent toward Christ.
Real faith may stumble.
It may tremble.
It may cry.
It may need correction, restoration, and forgiveness again and again.
But real faith does not regard Jesus as merely a convenient way to escape judgment while rejecting His rightful authority.
Grace does not mean sin has become harmless.
Grace means sinners can be forgiven and transformed.
Paul himself makes this unmistakable.
In Romans 6:1–2, he asks:
“What shall we say then? Shall we continue in sin, that grace may abound? God forbid. How shall we, that are dead to sin, live any longer therein?” (KJV)
Think about that.
The same Paul who declares justification by faith apart from works also rejects the idea that grace gives Christians permission to continue comfortably in sin.
And the same James who insists that faith without works is dead also teaches that salvation is rooted in God's gracious initiative.
James 1:18 says:
“Of his own will begat he us with the word of truth.” (KJV)
James does not imagine human goodness creating spiritual life.
He recognizes that new life comes from God.
So Paul and James are not standing on opposite sides of the Gospel.
They are confronting different distortions of it.
Paul is tearing down the illusion that works can earn salvation.
James is tearing down the illusion that a lifeless profession is the same as saving faith.
And then something extraordinary happens.
Both apostles bring us to the same man.
Abraham.
Paul writes in Romans 4:3:
James writes in James 2:21:
At first glance, the tension seems to return.
But look at the chronology.
Genesis 15:6 records Abraham believing God, and that faith being counted to him as righteousness.
Genesis 22 records Abraham's willingness to offer Isaac in obedience to God's command.
These events did not happen on the same day.
Abraham was counted righteous through faith before the later test involving Isaac.
And James explicitly recognizes that relationship.
In James 2:22–23, he writes:
The Greek word translated perfect in verse 22 comes from τελειόω (teleioō), which can mean to bring to completion or fulfillment.
James is describing Abraham's faith reaching its mature expression through obedience.
His obedience did not travel backward through time and purchase the righteousness already credited to him.
Rather, his actions demonstrated the living reality of the faith he professed.
There is also an important nuance in the word justify.
The Greek verb δικαιόω (dikaioō) can be used in contexts involving declaring someone righteous or vindicating and demonstrating righteousness.
Paul's argument in Romans 3–4 concerns how sinners are counted righteous before God apart from works of the law.
James's argument in James 2 concerns the vindication and completion of genuine faith through action.
The same Greek verb does not require the two writers to be addressing precisely the same issue in every passage.
Their surrounding arguments determine how their statements should be understood.
And there is another detail that should not be missed.
When Paul says “works of the law,” the Greek expression is ἔργων νόμου (ergōn nomou).
When James speaks of “works,” he uses forms of ἔργον (ergon), referring to deeds or actions.
Their vocabulary overlaps, but their arguments have different targets.
Paul rejects works as the basis on which sinners establish their righteousness before God.
James rejects a claim to faith that produces no corresponding obedience or mercy.

This distinction does not eliminate every historical theological debate about these passages. Christians across traditions have interpreted aspects of justification and the relationship between faith and works differently.
But the central point is clear from the texts themselves.
Neither apostle gives us permission to boast in our deeds.
Neither apostle gives us permission to treat obedience as irrelevant.
And neither apostle directs us away from Christ.
Now listen carefully, because this may be the sentence you need to remember when fear begins whispering that you will never be good enough.
Good works are not the price of salvation. They are the fruit of a life being transformed by God's grace.
Not the purchase price.
The fruit.
Not the foundation.
The result.
Not the Savior.
The evidence of His work.
And Paul says something remarkably similar.
Most people quote Ephesians 2:8–9 and stop there.
But verse 10 continues:
“For we are his workmanship, created in Christ Jesus unto good works, which God hath before ordained that we should walk in them.” (KJV)
Do you see the order?
Saved by grace through faith.
Not by works.
Created in Christ Jesus for good works.
Grace comes first.
Transformation follows.
The same passage that rules out boasting in good works also declares that good works belong to God's purpose for those He saves.
Paul and James are not competing.
They are helping us see the whole picture.
And Jesus Himself taught that a tree is known by its fruit.
In Matthew 7:17, He says:
“Even so every good tree bringeth forth good fruit; but a corrupt tree bringeth forth evil fruit.” (KJV)
Fruit does not create the tree.
It reveals the nature of the tree.
But be careful here.
This truth was never intended to turn every struggling believer into a prisoner of endless self-examination.
If you belong to Christ and are fighting a sin you hate, your struggle does not automatically mean your faith is false.
If you have repented and still feel the weight of past shame, that shame is not greater than the sufficiency of Jesus' sacrifice.
If you are growing slowly, God has not forgotten how to be patient.
Spiritual fruit grows through dependence on Christ, not through self-sufficient religious performance.
Jesus says in John 15:5:
“I am the vine, ye are the branches: He that abideth in me, and I in him, the same bringeth forth much fruit: for without me ye can do nothing.” (KJV)
Without Me.
Not without your perfect record.
Not without your impressive reputation.
Not without your ability to convince everyone that you have your life together.
Without Me.
That is the heart of it.
The Christian life does not begin with dependence on Jesus and then graduate into independence from Him.
It begins with grace.
It continues through grace.
And it ends in the glory of the Savior who holds His people fast.
Now imagine two people sitting in the same church.
The first is a woman who has spent years trying to prove she deserves God's love.
She serves every weekend.
She gives generously.
She rarely misses a service.
But when she lies in bed at night, she feels exhausted.
Every mistake becomes another accusation.
Every weakness becomes another reason to question whether God will accept her.
She knows the language of grace, but deep inside, she still believes she must earn her place at the Father's table.
Paul has something to tell her.
You cannot purchase what Jesus has already paid for.
Come to Christ.
Trust His finished work.
Let your obedience grow out of gratitude rather than terror.
Now imagine the second person.
He calls himself a Christian.
He knows the worship songs.
He shares Bible verses online.
He says salvation is by grace.
But he has no interest in repentance.
He refuses to confront his dishonesty.
He continues mistreating people without remorse.
He has turned “God knows my heart” into a shield against the very truth that could lead him to freedom.
James has something to tell him.
Do not confuse knowing Christian words with possessing living faith.
Do not mistake religious familiarity for spiritual surrender.
Do not use grace to silence the call of Jesus to follow Him.
Both people need the same Savior.
But they need to hear different warnings.
One needs to stop trying to earn God's acceptance.
The other needs to stop pretending that God's acceptance makes transformation unnecessary.
And perhaps the most uncomfortable realization is that both tendencies can exist in the same heart.
You may condemn yourself for one failure while excusing another sin you refuse to surrender.
You may be proud of your service while neglecting mercy.
You may defend salvation by grace with your mouth while secretly believing God loves you more on your best days.
That is why Scripture must be allowed to correct us.
Not merely confirm what we already want to believe.
Because the Gospel is not a mirror designed to flatter us.
It is the announcement of what God has done through Jesus Christ to rescue sinners and make them new.
And now we come to one of the most astonishing details in James's argument.
He brings up demons.
James 2:19 says:
“Thou believest that there is one God; thou doest well: the devils also believe, and tremble.” (KJV)
That verse should make every person who relies solely on intellectual agreement stop and think.
Demons know that God exists.
They are not atheists.
They possess correct knowledge about His reality.
But their knowledge is not saving trust in Jesus Christ.
James is exposing the difference between merely acknowledging religious facts and having genuine faith.
Knowing that Jesus is the Savior is not the same as personally trusting Him as Savior and Lord.
Knowing the Gospel is not the same as receiving it.
And knowing the language of repentance is not the same as turning to God.
This does not mean faith must reach a certain emotional intensity before God will accept you.
Saving faith is not measured by how dramatically you cry, how eloquently you pray, or how powerful your testimony sounds.
The object of faith matters.
Jesus Christ.
The crucified and risen Lord.
The One who saves.
And because He is alive, the faith that unites us to Him is not meant to remain spiritually lifeless.
His grace changes our relationship with sin, with others, and with God.
Sometimes that change is visible through extraordinary sacrifice.
Sometimes it appears in something as ordinary as telling the truth when lying would be easier.
Returning what you stole.
Apologizing without making excuses.
Feeding someone who cannot repay you.
Refusing to abandon your family.
Forgiving someone while still maintaining necessary boundaries.
Confessing a hidden sin.
Seeking help for a destructive habit.
Choosing integrity when nobody is watching.
Not to purchase salvation.
But because Jesus is teaching your heart to walk in a new direction.
And when you fail?
You do not return to the cross to ask Jesus to die again.
You return to the Savior whose sacrifice is sufficient.
You confess.
You repent.
You receive His mercy.
You get up and continue following Him.
First John 1:9 promises:
“If we confess our sins, he is faithful and just to forgive us our sins, and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness.” (KJV)
There is no need to pretend you are sinless.
But there is also no reason to make peace with the sin Christ came to deliver you from.
This is where grace becomes more than a word printed on a church banner.
It becomes the reason a broken person can begin again.
Maybe you are reading this with a history you wish you could erase.
Maybe your marriage has been damaged by decisions you regret.
Maybe you have betrayed someone's trust.
Maybe you have spent years hiding behind religious appearances.
Maybe you were once passionate about Jesus, but somewhere along the way your heart became cold.
Or maybe you are simply tired.
Tired of promising to change.
Tired of failing.
Tired of wondering whether God has finally run out of patience with you.
Hear the invitation of Christ.
Matthew 11:28 says:
“Come unto me, all ye that labour and are heavy laden, and I will give you rest.” (KJV)
He does not say, “Make yourself worthy, and then come.”
He says, “Come.”
But His invitation is not an invitation to remain chained to everything destroying you.
It is an invitation to come to the One who gives rest and teaches us to follow Him.
Jesus receives sinners.
And Jesus transforms sinners.
That is why our message has never been that your scandal is stronger than your Savior.
It is that grace can reach into the very places where shame convinced you your story was finished.
Peter's denial was not the end of Peter.
The persecutor Saul did not remain the persecutor Saul.
The thief beside Jesus had no lifetime of good works to present as the price of paradise, yet he appealed to the mercy of the crucified King.
And Jesus answered him with a promise.
“To day shalt thou be with me in paradise.” — Luke 23:43 (KJV)
The thief could not climb down from his cross and build a record of religious achievements.
His hope was in Jesus.
That is grace.
But the grace that saved him was not an endorsement of the life he had lived.
He acknowledged his guilt and recognized the innocence and kingship of Christ.
That is the difference.
Grace does not call evil good.
Grace offers forgiveness to those who have done evil.
And through Christ, it opens the door to a new life.
So when Paul says we are justified by faith apart from works of the law, listen.
When James says faith without works is dead, listen.
Do not silence one apostle to protect your preferred interpretation of the other.
Let both speak.
Let Paul strip away your pride in religious achievement.
Let James strip away your confidence in empty profession.
And let Jesus stand at the center of everything.
Because salvation is not a competition between Paul and James.
It is the work of the Father, through the Son, by the Holy Spirit, bringing sinners from death to life.
The cross answers our guilt.
The resurrection declares Christ's victory.
The Holy Spirit brings new life and produces fruit.
And genuine faith looks away from itself to the Savior who is worthy of trust.
If you remember nothing else from this article, remember this:
We are not saved because we do good works. We are saved by God's grace through faith in Jesus Christ, and the faith that truly receives Him is not meant to remain barren.
There is no room for boasting.
And there is no room for treating sin as a harmless companion.
There is only the Savior who justifies the ungodly and transforms those who belong to Him.
Perhaps that is why this message is so difficult to forget.
Because somewhere between Paul's warning and James's warning, we find ourselves.
The part of us that wants to earn God's love.
And the part of us that wants His blessings without surrender.
Both must come to the foot of the cross.
Both must bow before Jesus.
And both discover that the answer is not more confidence in ourselves.
It is deeper trust in Him.
Not for an argument.
Not for a religious performance.
But for an honest moment before God.
Which has been your greater struggle: trying to earn God's love through good works, or claiming to believe while resisting the changes Jesus is calling you to make?
You do not need to reveal private sins or painful details publicly. God knows what you are carrying, and you can seek confidential help from a trusted pastor or mature Christian when you need it.
Perhaps your words will also encourage someone else who thought they were the only one struggling.
And perhaps someone reading those comments will realize that repentance is not the end of hope.
It is part of returning to the One in whom hope is found.
If this article helped you understand Scripture more clearly, please save it.
There may come a night when you need to remember the difference between earning salvation and living out genuine faith.
Not because sharing a post makes anyone more righteous before God.
But because someone in your circle may be wrestling with these exact questions and may never have heard Paul and James explained together.
Invite them to read, ask questions, and return to the Bible for themselves.
And if you know someone who has walked away from the faith because Christianity seemed like an impossible list of rules, send this to them with kindness.
Let them see that the Gospel begins not with human achievement but with the saving work of Jesus Christ.
At Gospel Warrior, that is why we continue creating Christ-centered articles, biblical teaching, devotionals, and discipleship resources.
We want people to open their Bibles.
To ask difficult questions.
To examine familiar verses in context.
To understand the Gospel more deeply.
To turn from sin and find mercy in Christ.
To grow into mature believers whose lives reflect the Savior they profess.
And we want to make those resources available to as many people as possible.
Those free resources are part of our commitment to make biblical nourishment accessible, including to people who cannot afford paid materials.
Scripture tells us in 2 Corinthians 9:7:
“Every man according as he purposeth in his heart, so let him give; not grudgingly, or of necessity: for God loveth a cheerful giver.” (KJV)
Freely.
Prayerfully.
Without pressure or guilt.
Not to earn God's blessing.
Not to purchase salvation.
But because you believe this work is worth helping sustain and expand.
These products can serve as reminders of biblical truth, gifts of encouragement, and resources for continued spiritual growth.
Continue reading.
Continue learning.
Use the free resources.
Pray for the ministry.
Invite your family, friends, struggling believers, seekers, and even those who do not yet believe to explore the truth of the Gospel with us.
We are grateful for every person who supports the mission in whatever sincere and responsible way they can.
Because this has never been about building a following for its own sake.
It is about pointing people to Jesus.
The One who died for sinners.
The One who rose from the grave.
The One who offers forgiveness and calls us to repentance.
The One who receives the broken and makes them new.
And the One who will receive all the glory when our stories of redemption are finally told.
Paul was right.
James was right.
And Jesus is the reason their words belong together.
Faith is not a paycheck we hand to God.
Good works are not a ladder we climb to heaven.
Salvation is God's gracious gift in Christ, received through faith, and His transforming work bears fruit in the lives of His people.
So stop trying to buy what Christ freely offers.
And stop calling a life of deliberate spiritual indifference the fullness of saving faith.
Come to Jesus.
Trust Him.
Repent.
Abide in Him.
Follow Him.
And when you stumble, do not run away from the only One who can restore you.
Run back to Him.
Because the deepest scandal of the Gospel is not that sinners have failed.
It is that the sinless Son of God willingly gave Himself to rescue people who could never rescue themselves.
And the wonder of grace is that He does not merely forgive our past.
He gives us a new future in Himself.
The hands that could never earn your salvation are the very hands Jesus invites you to place in His—and the life you could never make righteous on your own is the life His grace can make new.
